memo: After reviewing the impact of the three possible actions for the 125 roles that can be automated, I have chosen to retrain and move all of them into plant positions at the plant‑role pay level (move_plant_pay). This path requires a one‑time investment of $15,000 per person for training materials and $45,600 for six months of pay and benefits, totaling $60,600 per employee. The Company already has a cash surplus of $44.1 million above the minimum operating level, so the $7.6 million required for the 125 retrainings can be comfortably funded. Once trained, each employee will be paid the plant average of $55,211, which is $16,560 less per year than their current average compensation. This generates a recurring annual saving of $2.07 million and, more importantly, supplies 125 of the 500 positions the plants need to fill, reducing external hiring costs and preserving valuable internal talent. Eliminating the roles would incur severance costs and lose the opportunity to meet plant staffing needs, while keeping current pay would increase ongoing payroll. Therefore, moving all 125 employees to plant roles delivers the best financial and strategic outcome.

The Company faces a strategic decision on how to handle the 125 roles that can be automated in Office & Administrative Support and Business & Financial Operations. Our analysis balances short‑term cash impact, long‑term cost savings, and the retention of valuable talent. 

We eliminate 30 positions, paying the modest severance of $8,902 per person ($267,000 total). This frees roughly $2.73 million of annual payroll and benefits, improving the cost base while keeping the one‑time cash outlay well within the $44.1 million cash cushion. 

We retrain and move 15 employees into plant roles while keeping their current compensation. The one‑time retraining and training‑pay cost is $60,600 per person ($909,000 total). This path preserves institutional knowledge and provides flexibility for future plant staffing needs, without immediate payroll savings. 

The bulk of the workforce – 80 employees – is retrained and moved into plant roles at the plant‑pay level. The one‑time cost of $60,600 per person totals $4.85 million, but it yields an annual payroll reduction of about $20,688 per employee, delivering roughly $1.66 million of yearly savings. Combined with the eliminations, the plan generates an estimated $4.38 million of annual cash‑flow improvement. 

Overall, the plan uses $6.02 million of the available cash surplus, leaves a comfortable $38 million buffer, and positions the Company for a leaner, more productive cost structure while retaining a core of experienced staff for future growth.

After reviewing the financial impact of the three possible paths for the 125 roles that can be automated, the elimination option provides the greatest net benefit to the Company. Severance for all 125 employees costs only $1.1 million, a one‑time cash outlay that is well within the $44.1 million cash cushion above the minimum operating level. Once eliminated, the Company saves the full payroll and benefits associated with these roles—$11.4 million annually—improving operating cash flow and strengthening the balance sheet. The alternative paths require substantial upfront retraining costs ($15,000 per person) and ongoing payroll expenses. Moving employees to plant roles at their current pay adds $16,560 per person per year in extra cost, while moving them to plant‑pay still incurs $7.6 million in one‑time training expenses and only modest annual savings ($2.1 million). Neither alternative offsets the immediate cash outlay or delivers the long‑term cash generation of outright elimination. Moreover, the automation technology fully replaces the work of these 125 positions, making the roles redundant. Therefore, we will eliminate all 125 positions, pay the $1.1 million severance, and realize the $11.4 million annual cost reduction, preserving cash and enhancing shareholder value.

After reviewing the three possible paths for the 125 roles that can be automated, the financial implications are clear. Eliminating the positions generates the greatest annual payroll savings ($8.97 million) while requiring only a one‑time severance outlay of about $1.1 million. The alternative of retraining and moving staff to plant roles at plant‑pay would cost $7.58 million up‑front and deliver only $2.07 million of yearly savings, and keeping current pay after retraining would actually increase ongoing payroll costs. With $44.1 million of cash above the minimum operating level, the company can comfortably fund the severance payment, and the net cash‑flow benefit of $7.86 million in the first year (and thereafter) strengthens the balance sheet and provides flexibility for future investments or shareholder returns. While retaining some staff could preserve institutional knowledge, the automation capability fully replaces the work of these functions, making the elimination the most fiscally responsible choice. Therefore, we will eliminate all 125 roles, pay the required severance, and reallocate the resulting payroll savings to support growth initiatives and maintain a strong liquidity position.

After reviewing the board pack and the new AI‑driven automation that can replace 125 roles in Office & Administrative Support (70 positions) and Business & Financial Operations (55 positions), I have chosen a mix of role elimination and redeployment that maximises cash efficiency while preserving operational capability. 

All 70 Office & Administrative Support positions are eliminated with severance. The one‑time severance cost of $8,902 per employee totals $0.62 million, and the company immediately saves $56,050 per former employee each year – a $3.92 million annual reduction in payroll. 

The 55 Business & Financial Operations staff are retrained and moved into plant roles at the plant‑average pay of $55,211. Retraining costs $15,000 per person plus $45,600 of pay/benefits during the six‑month training, amounting to $60,600 per employee, or $3.33 million in total one‑time outlay. Once placed, each employee’s salary falls by $36,569, delivering a $2.01 million annual payroll saving. 

No employees are kept on the higher‑pay plant‑role path, as that would add a recurring $16,560 per person cost and erode the cash benefit. The combined immediate cash requirement of $3.96 million is well within the $44.1 million cash buffer above the minimum operating level, and the ongoing annual savings of $5.93 million improve the company’s cost structure. This balanced approach aligns with the company’s financial discipline while leveraging the automation opportunity.

After reviewing the three possible pathways for the 125 roles that have become redundant due to recent AI automation, I have chosen to eliminate all of them. The elimination path requires a one‑time severance outlay of roughly $1.1 million, which is comfortably covered by the $44.1 million cash buffer above the minimum operating level. More importantly, it removes the ongoing payroll burden of $71,771 per employee per year (the weighted average of office‑admin and business‑finance salaries). This yields an annual cash saving of about $9.0 million, far exceeding the modest $2.1 million annual cost that would arise if the staff were retrained and kept at their current pay, and also surpasses the $2.1 million annual saving from retraining and moving them to plant‑pay roles. The company can therefore improve its cost structure, maintain a strong liquidity position, and avoid the additional training expenses ($60,600 per person) associated with the other two options. The decision also aligns with the strategic shift toward automation, ensuring the workforce is right‑sized for the new operating model while delivering the greatest financial benefit to shareholders.

After reviewing the three possible pathways for the 125 roles that have become redundant, the Board’s primary responsibility is to protect the Company’s financial health while respecting the cash cushion we have. Eliminating the positions delivers the greatest long‑term cash benefit: a one‑time severance outlay of roughly $1.1 million and an ongoing reduction of $11.4 million in payroll and benefits, the full cost of the work that is now automated. The alternative paths would require substantial upfront retraining expenses ($15 k per person plus $45.6 k of training payroll) and, in the case of moving employees at current pay, would increase annual cash outflows by about $2 million. Even the most favorable retraining option (moving to plant pay) still costs $7.6 million up‑front and only saves $2.1 million per year, far less than the $11.4 million saved by outright elimination. With $44.1 million of cash above the minimum operating level and a $300 million undrawn credit facility, we can comfortably fund the severance without jeopardising liquidity. Since the Board has not set a specific strategic objective beyond preserving value, the most prudent course is to eliminate all 125 roles, capture the full annual savings, and avoid unnecessary retraining costs.

The Company faces a clear opportunity to re‑allocate resources from support functions that can now be automated.  Our decision balances three priorities: preserving valuable talent where possible, minimizing one‑time cash outlays, and generating the greatest sustainable cash‑flow benefit.  We therefore eliminate 30 roles, paying the modest $8,900 severance per person.  This frees roughly $2.73 million of annual payroll while keeping the one‑time cost well within the $44.1 million cash buffer.  Fifteen employees are retrained and moved to plant roles but retain their current compensation.  This path incurs a one‑time $60,600 per person for training and pay during the six‑month period, but it preserves institutional knowledge that can be leveraged on the shop floor.  The bulk of the re‑allocation – 80 employees – are retrained and moved to plant positions at the plant‑pay rate.  This also costs $60,600 per person up‑front, yet it reduces ongoing payroll by an average $20,700 per employee each year, delivering an estimated $1.66 million in annual savings.  In total, the plan requires about $6.0 million of cash now and creates roughly $4.4 million of recurring cash‑flow improvement, comfortably supported by the existing cash surplus.  The mix respects the automation potential, retains critical expertise, and aligns the workforce with the Company’s long‑term operational focus.

The Board has identified 125 roles in Office & Administrative Support (70) and Business & Financial Operations (55) that can be replaced by AI. To preserve the existing functional mix, the allocation follows the 14:11 ratio (office:business) inherent in the 70:55 split. We therefore eliminate 50 positions (28 office, 22 business), retrain and move 50 employees into plant roles at the plant pay rate (28 office, 22 business), and retrain and move 25 employees into plant roles while retaining their current compensation (14 office, 11 business). 

Financially, the elimination saves roughly $3.6 M of base payroll (plus $0.96 M in benefits) and incurs $0.45 M in severance. The 50 employees moving to plant pay generate a one‑time retraining outlay of $750 k and $2.28 M of training payroll, but reduce ongoing salary costs by about $0.83 M per year. The 25 employees keeping current pay cost $375 k in retraining, $1.14 M in training payroll, and add $0.41 M per year in salary expense. Total immediate cash required is under $5 M, well within the $44.1 M cash cushion. Over the longer term, the net annual cash‑flow benefit is approximately $5 M, strengthening liquidity while maintaining the required skill mix across the two functions.

After reviewing the impact of the new AI tools that can automate 25% of the work in Office and Administrative Support and Business and Financial Operations, we have decided to eliminate all 125 affected roles. The AI solution fully replaces the functions performed by these employees, allowing us to capture the $11.4 million annual payroll and benefits savings. The one‑time severance outlay of $1.1 million is modest relative to the ongoing cash benefit and can be comfortably funded from the $44.1 million cash cushion above the minimum operating level. Eliminating the roles also simplifies the organization, reduces overhead, and improves our cost structure without compromising service delivery, as the AI system will maintain the required operational capacity. Retraining or retaining staff at higher cost would generate additional expenses and only modest payroll reductions, which do not outweigh the clear financial advantage of full elimination. This decision aligns with our commitment to prudent capital allocation, strengthens our balance sheet, and positions the Company for continued profitability and shareholder value creation.
